label: Bragg's law on a cubic lattice: the (100), (110), (111) glancing angles have sines in the ratio 1 : √2 : √3
statement_en: Bragg's condition for a reflection of order n is n λ = 2 d sin θ. In a cubic lattice of edge a the (hkl) planes are a/√(h²+k²+l²) apart, so for one order and one wavelength the sines of the glancing angles from the (100), (110) and (111) planes stand as 1 : √2 : √3. This ratio is what W. L. Bragg measured in 1913 to tell the face-centred from the simple cubic arrangement.

hypotheses.name: bragg-cubic-ratio#assumed-1
hypotheses.statement: Each reflection satisfies Bragg's condition n λ = 2 d sin θ with the plane spacing d of a cubic lattice of edge a > 0 (d = a/√(h²+k²+l²)). The condition itself (Bragg 1913) is taken as the model of reflection; the theorem does not derive it from wave optics.

hypotheses.name: bragg-cubic-ratio#assumed-2
hypotheses.statement: The same order n and wavelength λ for the three reflections.

scope.basis: a theorem about Bragg's condition on an ideal cubic lattice; the measured spacings of rock salt and calcite are separate data tests (bragg1915-01, bragg1915-06)
kernelChecked: Exact: with BraggReflects n λ (dSpacing a h k l) θ, sin θ = n λ √(h²+k²+l²) / (2a) (sin_of_bragg).
Exact: sin θ₁₁₀ = √2 sin θ₁₀₀ and sin θ₁₁₁ = √3 sin θ₁₀₀ (bragg_ratio).
Non-vacuity: a = 1, n = 1, λ = 2, θ = π/2 on (100) satisfies the condition (bragg_ratio_witness).
assumed: Bragg's condition n λ = 2 d sin θ as the model of reflection.
Cubic lattice of edge a > 0; same order and wavelength across the three reflections.
